stories.headline: FBI investigates apparent hack of its national crime database
stories.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, the database police across the country use to check for fugitives, missing persons, criminal histories and stolen property, according to an Associated Press report citing a single source. President Trump said Saturday the breach was "not good" but could let the government learn things it otherwise would not have. What was taken, and by whom, has not been made public in the coverage available.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the system an officer queries during a traffic stop or a missing-person search, and it holds sensitive records about millions of people. A breach could expose personal data or undermine confidence in records that police rely on every day.
stories.background: The National Crime Information Center, or NCIC, is a computerized index run by the FBI and shared with local, state and federal law enforcement. It began operating in 1967 and covers wanted persons, missing persons, criminal history data and stolen property. The FBI has disclosed other security incidents this year: in September it said it was investigating a hacking group's claim to have stolen employee data through its jobs website. CNBC described the NCIC incident as the second recent intrusion into FBI systems.

facts.text: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database, the Associated Press reported, citing a source.

stories.headline: Trump orders federal contractors to consult White House before answering Congress
stories.summary: President Trump signed an executive order Saturday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold communications the White House considers privileged. The White House warned that companies that do not comply could lose their contracts and be suspended from future federal work. The order comes weeks before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
stories.why_it_matters: Private companies do a large share of the government's work, and Congress often learns how taxpayer money is spent by asking them directly. The order could limit what lawmakers, and through them the public, find out. In today's ingest the story was carried almost entirely by left-leaning and center outlets.
stories.background: Democrats won control of Congress in this month's midterm elections and are expected to open wide-ranging investigations of the administration when they take over in January. Congressional committees can request or subpoena documents from companies that hold federal contracts. Presidents can claim executive privilege to keep some internal communications from Congress, and disputes over its reach are usually settled by negotiation or in court. Several outlets describe the order as the administration's latest step to resist that expected oversight.

stories.headline: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card rates at 10%
stories.summary: President Trump said Saturday he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, repeating a call he first made in January. He said in a phone interview that card companies make too much money and that he "would do it." No bill or timetable was reported.
stories.why_it_matters: The typical card rate is around 22%, so a 10% cap would sharply cut interest costs for people who carry a balance. Banks have argued a cap would lead them to offer less credit, especially to riskier borrowers.
stories.background: Trump called in January for a one-year, 10% cap on credit card interest and later asked Congress to pass it, but no cap took effect. Sens. Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley had earlier introduced a bipartisan bill for a 10% cap. Banking groups opposed the idea, saying it would reduce access to credit. Democrats won control of Congress in this month's midterms and take over in January.

stories.headline: Immigration officers arrest two passengers on Seattle airport jet bridge
stories.summary: Masked immigration officers arrested two people on a crowded jet bridge at Seattle's airport Saturday as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, delaying the flight. Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle both called the scene distressing, and the port said local authorities would ask federal officials what happened. stories.background: The Trump administration has stepped up immigration enforcement nationwide, and attorneys said earlier this year that arrests at airports were becoming more frequent. Seattle-Tacoma International Airport is run by the Port of Seattle, a local public agency that says it has no jurisdiction over Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations there.

stories.headline: Appeals court says law protecting pregnant workers was passed unconstitutionally
stories.summary: The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a law protecting pregnant workers was passed unconstitutionally because House members voted by proxy during the Covid pandemic, The New York Times reported. The ruling halts the law, and the case is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court. CNN and The Washington Post described the decision as striking at the wider spending law that contained the protections.
stories.why_it_matters: The law requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for pregnant workers, and those protections are now in question. The reasoning could also be used to challenge other laws passed while the House allowed proxy voting. Only left-leaning outlets in today's ingest covered the ruling.
stories.background: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was passed at the end of 2022 as part of a large government spending bill, at a time when House rules let absent members cast votes through colleagues. Texas sued, arguing that the Constitution requires a majority of members to be physically present to pass legislation. A federal judge in Texas agreed in 2024 and blocked the law's enforcement against the state as an employer. A three-judge Fifth Circuit panel reversed that decision in August 2025, and the court then took up the case again.

The decision is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court, according to The New York Times.

stories.summary: San Francisco's mayor asked residents not to travel unless "absolutely essential" as Northern California prepares for heavy rain arriving with unusually high tides. Florida has separately been dealing with flooding from a major storm system.

stories.headline: Jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire
stories.summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty of arson charges for starting the January 2025 Palisades Fire, which killed 12 people. stories.why_it_matters: The fire was one of the most destructive in Los Angeles history, and the verdict is a formal finding of who was responsible for a disaster that destroyed thousands of homes.
stories.background: The Palisades Fire broke out in January 2025 and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in and around the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles. Federal prosecutors charged Rinderknecht, a former rideshare driver, with arson. His first trial ended in June when the jury deadlocked, with 10 of 12 jurors favoring acquittal according to the Associated Press, and the judge set a retrial at prosecutors' request.

stories.headline: Mexico captures cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in a raid that left at least 11 dead
stories.summary: Mexican authorities said they captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a cartel leader known as 'El Chapo Isidro', in Sinaloa state on Saturday. The operation set off gun battles that left at least 11 people dead. He was on the FBI's list of 10 most wanted fugitives. The reports available did not say whether or when he might be sent to the United States.
stories.why_it_matters: His organization is accused of sending large amounts of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States for two decades. The arrest also shows how closely Mexican and U.S. agencies are now working together against cartels, and how violent those operations can be for people living nearby.
stories.background: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores is a drug trafficker from Sinaloa, the Pacific coast state that is home to several of Mexico's biggest criminal groups. His nickname echoes Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman, the former Sinaloa Cartel leader now in a U.S. prison, but the two are different men. He is accused of drug trafficking and torture, and the FBI placed him on its Ten Most Wanted list, with a U.S. reward of up to $5 million. His capture follows a string of arrests of senior drug traffickers in Mexico.

stories.headline: UN climate talks run two days over as final draft leaves out fossil fuels
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Turkey went into a second day of overtime on Sunday. Turkey's final draft deal does not mention fossil fuels, and the European Union and a group of other countries have refused to endorse it. Summit president Murat Kurum gave delegates about three hours to object before putting the text to the full conference; the outcome was not known in the reports available.
stories.why_it_matters: The yearly UN summit sets the direction for how quickly countries cut the pollution that drives heat waves, floods and higher insurance and food costs. A deal that does not name oil, gas and coal, or no deal at all, would signal that governments remain split on the main cause of warming.
stories.background: COP31 is this year's UN climate conference, where nearly 200 countries negotiate by consensus. It is being held in Turkey, with Australia leading the negotiations under a shared hosting arrangement. In 2023 countries agreed for the first time to 'transition away' from fossil fuels, and the fight since has been over whether to say how and when. An early draft this week referred to fossil fuels, but a revised text published Thursday removed the reference while keeping a goal to raise electricity's share of energy use. The EU and about a dozen other countries want clear fossil fuel language; the Financial Times describes the EU as in a direct clash with Saudi Arabia over the text.

Divisions also remain over climate finance and global warming targets, France 24 reported.

stories.headline: Russian cargo ship burns off Finland after drone strike; Finland says the war is 'spilling over'
stories.summary: A Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad was hit by drones in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters, where it was still burning on Sunday. The crew was evacuated. Finland's defence forces said Ukraine was probably behind the attack, and Finland restricted air and sea traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland and said it suspects a Russian helicopter then violated its airspace.
stories.why_it_matters: The strike happened next to a NATO member's coast, far from the front line, and Finland's government is openly warning that the Ukraine war is reaching its territory. That raises the risk of an incident between Russia and NATO and of disruption to Baltic shipping.
stories.background: The Gulf of Finland is the narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland, Estonia and Russia, and it is Russia's sea route from St Petersburg to its Kaliningrad exclave. Finland joined NATO in 2023 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine has used long-range drones against Russian ports and ships in the Baltic, and Finland said on Nov. 13 that it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area. stories.headline: South Korea's education minister resigns over AI cheating scandal and exam-day checks
stories.summary: South Korea's education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, resigned on Sunday, saying he had failed to prepare adequately for this week's national college entrance exam. stories.headline: Tech stocks close their worst week since 2020 as doubts about AI spending spread
stories.summary: US stocks fell sharply again last week, with technology shares posting what CNBC called their worst week on Wall Street since 2020. Investors sold AI-linked companies even after Nvidia reported earnings and Anthropic completed a record stock offering. This week is shortened by Thanksgiving, with reports on economic growth and inflation due Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: Big technology companies make up a large share of the index funds in most retirement accounts, so a prolonged drop in those shares shows up directly in 401(k) balances.
stories.background: For about three years, stock gains have been led by companies building or supplying artificial intelligence, especially the chipmaker Nvidia. This month investors began questioning whether the hundreds of billions being spent on data centers will pay off, and the Nasdaq fell more than 10 percent from its October high, a drop traders call a correction. The selling deepened after Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned on Nov. 12. Last week brought two events that some investors hoped would steady things, Nvidia's quarterly results and Anthropic's stock market debut, but shares kept falling.

stories.summary: South Korea's top financial officials held an emergency meeting on Sunday and announced step-by-step measures to calm markets, including having a stock stabilization fund ready, Bloomberg reported. Shares in Tokyo and Seoul fell steeply on Nov. 6 after a US tech sell-off. A stabilization fund is a pool of money, usually put up by financial institutions at the government's request, that buys shares when prices are falling fast. A margin requirement is the amount of an investor's own money needed to borrow for stock purchases; lowering it makes borrowing easier.

stories.headline: Families fault the city at a vigil as questions grow over oversight before the Flatbush collapse
stories.summary: Ten days after a building on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn collapsed and killed eight people, relatives of the victims criticized city officials at a Saturday vigil at the site. The New York Times reported that experts say the Buildings Department had approved a risky method of shoring up the structure, which stood next to a construction site. The city says the damaged building next door must also be torn down, and its residents and neighbors are waiting to learn what comes next.
stories.why_it_matters: Many New Yorkers live beside construction sites, and this case tests whether the city's reviews and inspections protect the people next door. The answers could change how excavation and demolition near occupied buildings are approved.
stories.background: On Nov. 11 a three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed; it stood beside a lot where a new development was under construction. Eight people died, and the Fire Department has ended its recovery work. The Department of Buildings, the city agency that reviews construction plans and inspects sites, had previously cited the neighboring construction site, according to trade press reports. The department has since declared the adjoining building at 1323 Flatbush Avenue beyond repair and ordered it demolished. The cause of the collapse has not been officially determined.

stories.summary: A federal judge on Friday denied a request to release Oscar Belgal, a Dominican man who was shot and wounded by immigration officers as they arrested him in New York in October. markets.summary: U.S. markets were closed for the weekend after what CNBC called technology's worst week on Wall Street since 2020. The S&P 500 and the Dow ended Friday in a correction, meaning at least 10% below their recent highs, as investors sold companies tied to artificial intelligence; Nvidia finished its longest run of weekly losses since 2008, CNBC reported, days after Anthropic's record initial public offering. The selling spread to Asia, where Japan's Nikkei 225 fell about 5% on Friday. Over the weekend governments stepped in: South Korea's financial officials held an emergency meeting on Sunday and said a stock stabilization fund, a pool of money that can buy shares to steady prices, would be kept ready, and China loosened the rules on borrowing to buy stocks, Bloomberg reported. concept.explanation: Buying on margin means borrowing money from a broker to buy stocks, putting up only part of the price yourself. The margin requirement is the share you must cover with your own cash; regulators and brokers raise it to cool speculation and lower it, as China did this weekend, to encourage buying. Borrowing magnifies gains when prices rise, but when they fall the broker can demand more cash or sell your shares, a "margin call," and those forced sales can push a falling market down faster. Even if you never borrow to invest, that chain reaction can deepen the swings in a retirement account that holds stock funds.
